meta.title: Who really said "The world of reality has its limits; the world of imagination is boundless"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, it's Rousseau — from Émile (1762), Book II, in Barbara Foxley's 1911 translation. But he meant it as a warning against imagination, not a celebration of it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The world of reality has its limits; the world of imagination is boundless'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Rousseau, from Émile Book II (Foxley's 1911 translation) — but quoted to mean the opposite of what he argued.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From ‘Émile, ou De l’éducation’ (1762), Book II. Barbara Foxley’s standard 1911 English translation reads “The world of reality has its bounds, the world of imagination is boundless” — the popular version simply swaps “bounds” for “limits.” The wording is genuinely his; the inspirational spin is not.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Émile, ou De l’éducation, Book II
“Le monde réel a ses bornes, le monde imaginaire est infini”

source.excerpt: The world of reality has its bounds, the world of imagination is boundless; as we cannot enlarge the one, let us restrict the other; for all the sufferings which really make us miserable arise from the difference between the real and the imaginary.
trail: The quote is unanimously credited to Rousseau across quote sites such as BrainyQuote, but they cite no work — the usual signature of an unsourced attribution.
The thought traces to Émile, Book II, whose French reads “Le monde réel a ses bornes, le monde imaginaire est infini…”
A full-text search of Barbara Foxley’s 1911 English Émile returns the near-exact line: “The world of reality has its bounds, the world of imagination is boundless.”
The line appears in none of the sourced, disputed or misattributed sections of Wikiquote’s Rousseau page, so we verified it against the primary text directly.
source.excerptNote: Foxley’s 1911 translation, Émile Book II. Note the argument: because imagination is boundless, we should restrict it — the opposite of the “dream big” message the line is now used to carry.

sourceLink.text: Read Émile, Book II at Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: Émile was first published in 1762, and Barbara Foxley’s English translation in 1911 — both well before 1931, so both the French original and this translation are in the public domain in the United States. Project Gutenberg hosts the Foxley translation on that basis.

author.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
author.heading: About Jean-Jacques Rousseau
author.bio: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a Genevan-born philosopher, novelist and composer whose work shaped the Enlightenment, the French Revolution and modern political and educational thought. Émile (1762), his treatise on education framed as the upbringing of a fictional boy, and The Social Contract of the same year are his most influential books. A central theme across his work is that human unhappiness grows from the gap between our desires and our powers — the very idea behind this quotation.

misattribution.heading: The catch
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely Rousseau — the problem is not the author but the meaning and, slightly, the wording.

items.why: The line is shared as a celebration of limitless imagination. Rousseau argues the reverse: because “we cannot enlarge” reality, “let us restrict the other” — imagination’s boundlessness is the source of the desires that make us unhappy. See the full passage in Émile, Book II.
Barbara Foxley’s 1911 translation actually reads “has its bounds”; the popular version substitutes “limits.” The second half, “the world of imagination is boundless,” is verbatim Foxley.
A handful of quote pages tag the line to Einstein, drawn by his own imagination sayings, but there is no basis for it — the words are Rousseau’s via Foxley.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are really Rousseau’s, from Émile, Book II — but he wrote them to warn against imagination, not to cheer it on.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Rousseau’s point in this passage of Émile is a theory of happiness: misery, he says, “consists not in the lack of things, but in the needs which they inspire.” Since reality is fixed and imagination endlessly inflates our desires, the path to contentment is to shrink imagination back toward what we actually have.

Detached from that argument, the sentence became one of the internet’s favourite inspirational lines — a toast to boundless creativity. It is a striking example of a real, correctly-attributed quotation whose meaning has been flipped by the company it keeps.
context.pull: He wrote it to argue we should restrict imagination — not unleash it.
